title: IV: The Interview

teacherSummary.text: Back in prison Hester is frantic. The stranger, now calling himself Roger Chillingworth, a physician, calms the baby and Hester with medicines. He admits he wronged her by marrying her young, but vows to discover her lover. He makes her swear to keep his identity secret.

segments.script: Physicians were scarce in early Massachusetts; knowledge of herbs, including Native remedies, gave Chillingworth authority. Chillingworth's calm, rational revenge begins here and will make him the novel's worst sinner. Characterization: Chillingworth, now a physician, visits Hester in prison and calms Pearl with a draught. Foreshadowing: He vows to find the father: "Sooner or later, he must needs be mine!" Conflict: Husband and wife admit their mutual wrong; he extracts her promise of secrecy about his identity. Watch for the scarlet letter: The embroidered "A" changes meaning as the town and the reader watch it: adultery, then "Able," then something like "Angel," and finally an emblem Hester chooses to keep. In this chapter: “to the prison, Hester Prynne was found to be in a state of nervous excitement that demanded constant watchfulness, lest she should” (IV: The Interview, paragraph 1).

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Mine was the first wrong, when I betrayed thy budding youth into a false and unnatural relation with my decay” slowly and put it in my own words: Chillingworth tells Hester that he wronged her first by marrying her youth to his old age. Next, craft. I notice he contrasts "budding youth" with "my decay," images of spring and rot. The strongest word is “decay”: it shows how he sees himself, old and withered beside her. Then, effect. What does Chillingworth admit about his own guilt? My answer: Chillingworth admits his own guilt in marrying Hester, young and unloving, when he was old and misshapen; the admission makes him seem reasonable but sets up his cold plan to punish her partner.
